concepts.definition: Technologies where a foreign power has you by the throat — critical dependencies that can be weaponized.
concepts.insight: In Chinese public discourse this isn't abstract policy language — it's visceral. The ballpoint pen parable (a space-faring nation that couldn't make a pen tip) turned it into a national humiliation narrative that drives trillion-dollar investment decisions.
concepts.callbackVisual: 2s KineticTypography flash — 卡脖子 in rust with brief pinyin, no definition repeat

concepts.definition: China's mobilization model — concentrate national resources, tolerate waste, accept short-term inefficiency for long-term sovereignty.
concepts.insight: The same mindset that built the atomic bomb program, the space program, and the rail network. The question is whether it works for semiconductors, where the complexity is distributed across a global network rather than containable within a single national system.
concepts.callbackVisual: 2s KineticTypography — 举国体制 in rust, subtitle 'whole-nation system'

concepts.definition: Using export controls and supply chain leverage to prevent a rival from accessing critical technologies.
concepts.insight: Two historical precedents point in opposite directions — the 1941 oil embargo triggered the catastrophe it was meant to prevent, while COCOM kept the USSR 5-10 years behind for four decades. The country being denied this time resembles neither precedent.

appearances.notes: Technology denial reframed as a tragedy-of-the-commons problem — the denial mechanism itself creates defection incentives

concepts.callbackVisual: 3s TimelineComparison callback — 1941 and 2022 timelines briefly flash with key dates highlighted

concepts.definition: The US froze Japan's assets and cut off 80% of its oil supply to constrain military expansion — 134 days later, Japan attacked Pearl Harbor.
concepts.insight: Resource denial designed to prevent war triggered the exact catastrophe it was meant to avoid. The structural parallel to modern chip controls: constraining a rival's access to a critical resource can accelerate rather than prevent escalation.
concepts.callbackVisual: 2s TimelineComparison left-column flash — '1941: 134 days' in amber

concepts.definition: The Coordinating Committee for Multilateral Export Controls — 17 Western nations that restricted computing and advanced manufacturing to the Soviet Bloc for 45 years.
concepts.insight: The only precedent where technology denial worked for decades. But it worked because the USSR was economically isolated, technologically stagnant, and systemically dysfunctional — China is none of those things.
concepts.callbackVisual: 3s ChoroplethMap callback — 17 COCOM nations flash blue, then fade to present-day map

concepts.definition: A four-dimension comparison showing why technology denial worked against the USSR but faces structural obstacles against China.
concepts.insight: Across economic integration, talent recruitment, retaliatory leverage, and indigenous capability, China scores dramatically higher than the USSR — making the COCOM precedent misleading as a guide to modern export controls.
concepts.callbackVisual: 2s FrameworkDiagram — 4-dim comparison, highlight the dimension most relevant to current context

concepts.definition: Jake Sullivan's framing for US export controls — narrowly targeted restrictions with maximum enforcement. In practice, the yard kept expanding and the fence kept getting taller.
concepts.insight: The phrase reveals the internal contradiction of targeted denial: once you accept the logic of maintaining maximum technological lead, there's no principled place to stop expanding the scope of controls.
concepts.callbackVisual: 2s KineticTypography — 'small yard, high fence' in amber with yard-expansion animation

concepts.definition: Trump's August 2025 deal allowing Nvidia and AMD to sell AI chips to China in exchange for 15% of revenue going to the US government.
concepts.insight: Export controls — a national security instrument — became a tax. In three years, policy went from 'deny China access' to 'let China have access, but take a cut.' The trajectory reveals that economic incentives eventually overwhelm security logic.
concepts.callbackVisual: 2s KineticTypography — '20% → 15%' in amber

concepts.definition: $52.7 billion authorized to rebuild American semiconductor manufacturing — the largest industrial policy investment since the Interstate Highway System.
concepts.insight: The gap between authorized ($52.7B), awarded ($30.9B), and disbursed ($6B) reveals the structural difficulty of translating legislative ambition into manufacturing capacity. Trump called the program 'horrible.'
concepts.callbackVisual: 2s DataChart — funding funnel bars ($52.7B → $6B disbursed)

concepts.definition: The US plays chess — targeting specific pieces (companies, chokepoints). China plays go — surrounding territory stone by stone, accepting local losses for positional advantage.
concepts.insight: Both metaphors reveal strategic style, but the deeper insight is that both players are trapped. The extreme globalization that made chips cheap is exactly what makes them strategically vulnerable — and every attempt to reduce vulnerability undermines the efficiency that made chips matter.
concepts.callbackVisual: 3s split — chess board (left, US-blue) and go board (right, China-rust), pieces frozen mid-game

concepts.definition: The most complex supply chain humans have ever built — a single chip touches photoresists from Japan, lithography from the Netherlands, design software from California, packaging from Taiwan, rare earths from China. No country can replicate this alone.
concepts.insight: Full self-sufficiency would cost an estimated $1 trillion. The extreme globalization that made chips cheap, ubiquitous, and transformative is exactly what makes them strategically vulnerable. Every attempt to reduce that vulnerability undermines the efficiency that made chips matter. That's the trap — not for one side, for everyone.

appearances.notes: Referenced when discussing the Escrow State problem — ASML, SK Hynix, Samsung caught between US enforcement and Chinese market access

concepts.callbackVisual: 3s RouteAnimation — 6-country supply chain lines pulse, then one link flashes red

concepts.definition: Countries like the Netherlands (ASML), South Korea (Samsung/SK Hynix), and Japan (photoresist) that are being forced to pick sides in a conflict where either choice costs them enormously.
concepts.insight: ASML saw China drop from 36% to 20% of revenue. South Korea has $40B sunk in Chinese fabs. Japan controls 70% of global photoresist. These aren't bystanders — they're the load-bearing pillars of the supply chain, and they're being asked to choose which half of their business to sacrifice.

appearances.notes: Deepened into 'The Escrow State' — nations holding restricted technology with inherent defection incentives. Korea's Lee quote: 'can no longer maintain balance'

concepts.callbackVisual: 2s ChoroplethMap — Netherlands, South Korea, Japan highlighted amber

concepts.definition: The splitting of the technological world into two partially overlapping, partially incompatible ecosystems — one built on American architecture, one on Chinese alternatives.
concepts.insight: Chris Miller's 2022 prediction that looked most prescient by 2025. Not victory for either side — a splitting. Both ecosystems less efficient than the integrated system they replaced. Your next phone might not run the same apps as your colleague's in Shanghai.
concepts.callbackVisual: 3s RouteAnimation — supply chain map splitting into two diverging networks

concepts.definition: DeepSeek R1 proved Chinese AI could compete on inferior hardware. DeepSeek R2 couldn't complete a single training run on domestic chips. Both truths coexist.
concepts.insight: China can innovate brilliantly around constraints, and the constraints are real. The question that determines whether export controls succeed or fail is which of those truths has the longer half-life.
concepts.callbackVisual: 2s KineticTypography — 'R1: competitive. R2: 0 successful runs.' in rust

concepts.definition: SMIC achieves 7nm chips without EUV lithography by running 34 lithography passes where a Western fab uses 9 — more expensive, slower, and it works.
concepts.insight: The novel-by-typewriter analogy. Every extra pass is another defect chance, another cost multiplier. But yields went from below 40% to 60-70% by mid-2025. The ceiling is real (Kirin X90 was relabeled 7nm, not true 5nm) but the progress is also real.
concepts.callbackVisual: 2s DataChart — '34 vs 9 passes' bars in rust/amber

concepts.definition: The founder of TSMC — who built the globalized semiconductor supply chain — declaring that 'Globalization is almost dead. Free trade is almost dead.'
concepts.insight: The person who built the system being torn apart is the one saying it's over. This carries weight no analyst's opinion can match — it's the architect watching the demolition.
concepts.callbackVisual: 3s KineticTypography — Chang quote in bone on ink, amber attribution

concepts.definition: The unanswerable question that changes everything: if transformative AI arrives in 2-3 years, controls bought time; if it takes a decade, controls accomplished nothing except motivating Chinese self-sufficiency.
concepts.insight: This is the meta-uncertainty underneath the entire chip war debate. Most analysis assumes a fixed technology trajectory, but the value of export controls is entirely conditional on a timeline nobody can predict.
concepts.callbackVisual: 3s FrameworkDiagram — decision tree with 'Fast AI' and 'Slow AI' branches, uncertainty bars

concepts.definition: Until 2017, China could launch astronauts and build supercomputers but couldn't manufacture the steel ball at a pen tip — the symbol of humiliating technological dependence.
concepts.insight: When state media reported this, it crystallized everything about 卡脖子 into a single image. Chips are that story at civilizational scale — the contrast between massive achievement and tiny dependency.
concepts.callbackVisual: 1s image flash — pen tip macro with '2017' date stamp

concepts.definition: A formal method for revising probability estimates as new evidence arrives — starting with a prior belief, then systematically adjusting it with each new data point to produce a posterior.
concepts.insight: Most geopolitical commentary treats each new development as either confirming or refuting a thesis. Bayesian updating makes the *degree* of belief shift visible — some evidence barely moves the needle, other evidence is transformative. This turns prediction from binary to calibrated.
concepts.callbackVisual: BayesianUpdate template — distribution curve with episode-specific evidence items, amber accent

concepts.definition: When you tighten restrictions on a scarce resource, you increase the profit margin for breaking those restrictions — the enforcement mechanism creates the conditions for its own failure.
concepts.insight: This isn't a policy failure but a structural inevitability. The same mechanism shows up in COCOM (1949-1994), Venice's Murano glass monopoly (14th-17th c.), OPEC production quotas (1983-present), Atlantic fishing quotas, and nuclear non-proliferation. In every case, tighter enforcement increased defection incentives rather than reducing them.
concepts.callbackVisual: 3s DataChart — the Blockade Paradox curve (enforcement tightness vs defection incentive), rust accent

concepts.definition: When individual rational defections from a cooperative regime accumulate — each one destabilizes the regime slightly, triggering tighter enforcement, which creates higher payoff for the next defection.
concepts.insight: The cascade isn't coordinated. It's thousands of individual actors — chip brokers, logistics companies, traders — each making a rational expected-value calculation. If even 60-70% of smuggled shipments get through, defection is profitable. The regime tightens; the cascade accelerates.
concepts.callbackVisual: 2s KineticTypography — 'THE DEFECTION CASCADE' in rust, no definition repeat

concepts.definition: A nation or company that holds restricted technology on behalf of an enforcement coalition — with inherent economic incentives to defect if the arrangement becomes painful enough.
concepts.insight: ASML, South Korea, Japan aren't US agents — they're escrow holders with their own interests. SK Hynix and Samsung have ~$40B invested in Chinese fabs. When the cost of cooperation exceeds the benefit, the escrow holder defects. This is the alliance-level version of the individual smuggler's calculus.
concepts.callbackVisual: 2s KineticTypography — 'THE ESCROW STATE' in rust, with country flags briefly visible

concepts.definition: When individuals sharing a common resource each act in their own rational self-interest, the resource is depleted — individually rational, collectively catastrophic.
concepts.insight: Garrett Hardin named it in 1968 thinking about pastures, but the mechanism is the structural foundation of every technology-denial failure in history. The 'commons' in export controls is the cooperative regime itself — each defection degrades it, but each defector profits.
concepts.callbackVisual: 2s FrameworkDiagram — pasture with degradation indicator, amber accent

concepts.definition: A situation where two or more actors each have incentive to defect from cooperation, even though mutual cooperation would produce a better outcome for all.
concepts.insight: Not just a game-theory abstraction — it's the operational reality of every export control regime. The payoff matrix (cooperate and fall behind vs. defect and gain advantage) explains why COCOM leaked, why OPEC overproduces, why fishing quotas are exceeded, and why chip smuggling industrializes.
concepts.callbackVisual: 2s FrameworkDiagram — 2x2 payoff matrix with COOPERATE/DEFECT, amber accent

concepts.definition: Elinor Ostrom's research showing commons can be managed with clearly defined boundaries, monitoring, graduated sanctions, and legitimate dispute resolution where all members have voice.
concepts.insight: The path-not-taken for export controls. Ostrom showed commons governance *can* work — but it requires all members to have voice and formal dispute resolution. US export controls are unilateral; allies have no complaint mechanism. This structural gap explains why Ostrom's solution can't scale to great-power competition.
concepts.callbackVisual: 3s FrameworkDiagram — Ostrom's 8 principles with export control violations highlighted in rust

concepts.definition: China will not achieve commercial-scale 7nm chip production (>50,000 wafers/month) by Q4 2027.
concepts.insight: Export controls slow but don't stop. If SMIC can't scale 7nm by late 2027, controls bought at least one full generation of lead time — the threshold that matters for AI development windows.

prediction.claim: China will not achieve commercial-scale 7nm chip production (>50,000 wafers/month) by Q4 2027.
prediction.falsification: SMIC or another Chinese fab announces >50K wafers/month of 7nm-equivalent production, confirmed by TechInsights teardown or SMIC quarterly report.
prediction.whatWouldChangeMyMind: Credible TechInsights teardowns showing 7nm yields above 70% on Chinese-built chips in volume before 2027, or SMIC quarterly filings showing wafer-count growth inconsistent with anything but 7nm-scale operation.
watchSignals: SMIC quarterly earnings — wafer shipments by node
TechInsights teardowns of Huawei/Chinese-brand flagship chips
CSIS semiconductor tracker updates

term.en: Partial tech bifurcation as dominant outcome

concepts.definition: The US-China semiconductor dispute will produce partial bifurcation (two parallel ecosystems) rather than full decoupling or renewed convergence by 2028.
concepts.insight: Neither full victory nor full failure — the divergence without equilibrium outcome predicted by the Silicon Trap analysis. Clean resolution in either direction requires political will or catastrophe that current incentives make unlikely.

prediction.claim: The US-China semiconductor dispute will produce partial bifurcation — two parallel but not fully separate ecosystems — by 2028, rather than full decoupling or renewed convergence.
prediction.falsification: A major US-China semiconductor agreement substantially restoring cross-border chip flows is signed, OR full legal prohibition on all chip trade between US-allied supply chain and China takes effect.
prediction.whatWouldChangeMyMind: A Taiwan Strait military incident triggering emergency full decoupling, or a breakthrough US-China diplomatic deal that restores TSMC-China business relationships to pre-2022 levels.
watchSignals: US-China bilateral trade data — semiconductor category
TSMC cross-strait production allocation announcements
Huawei smartphone chipset sourcing reports
Kalshi: US-China trade war escalation contracts

concepts.definition: The US will not achieve 20% of world advanced-node semiconductor production domestically by 2030.
concepts.insight: The CHIPS Act committed $52.7B for a target requiring engineering feats not yet demonstrated at volume. TSMC Arizona yields are strong but volume and node advancement remain years behind Taiwan.

prediction.claim: The US will not achieve 20% of world advanced-node (sub-5nm) semiconductor production from domestic fabs by 2030.
prediction.falsification: TSMC Arizona, Intel 18A, or Samsung Texas collectively produce >20% of global sub-5nm wafer starts by 2030 Q1, per SIA or SEMI industry data.
prediction.whatWouldChangeMyMind: Intel 18A achieving >70% yield at volume by 2027, or TSMC Arizona N2 production beginning ahead of 2028 schedule.
watchSignals: TSMC Arizona quarterly production reports
Intel 18A yield announcements
SIA annual state-of-industry data
CHIPS Act milestone completion rate (GAO tracker)

concepts.definition: At least one G7 country will significantly weaken semiconductor export controls or secure major carve-outs by 2027, consistent with the Defection Cascade mechanism.
concepts.insight: The Blockade Paradox in action: tighter controls increase the profit from defection. The question is not whether defection happens but which ally defects first and how.

prediction.claim: At least one G7 country will formally weaken semiconductor export controls or secure major carve-outs (worth >$1B annual revenues to its companies) by Q4 2027.
prediction.falsification: All G7 members maintain or tighten semiconductor controls through 2027 with no carve-outs exceeding $500M annual revenue impact.
prediction.whatWouldChangeMyMind: Clear evidence that allied companies are not suffering significant revenue losses from controls, or a binding multilateral enforcement mechanism with real penalties.
watchSignals: ASML quarterly earnings — China revenue share and forward guidance
Dutch government ASML policy announcements
Japan METI export control review statements
South Korea semiconductor policy announcements
SK Hynix and Samsung China operations revenue disclosures

term.en: China chip self-sufficiency stays below 50% by 2028

concepts.definition: China's semiconductor self-sufficiency will remain below 50% of domestic demand by 2028, consistent with controls slowing but not stopping progress.
concepts.insight: The honest middle position: controls are not failing entirely (self-sufficiency is not accelerating past 50%) but are not succeeding entirely. 50% is the threshold where the strategic calculus changes — below it, China still depends on the global supply chain.

prediction.claim: China's semiconductor self-sufficiency (domestic production as share of domestic consumption) will remain below 50% by 2028.
prediction.falsification: CSIS semiconductor tracker, SEMI, or Chinese MIIT reports show China producing >50% of consumed chips domestically by 2028.
prediction.whatWouldChangeMyMind: Big Fund III delivering domestic fab capacity ahead of schedule, or an unexpected technology breakthrough enabling rapid SMIC scaling.
watchSignals: CSIS semiconductor self-sufficiency tracker (annual)
China MIIT announcements
SMIC, YMTC, CXMT quarterly capacity reports
Big Fund III capital deployment pace
